opus-5.5.text:
I think it's really a combination of both, and Motion Transfer is a good example of how the two need to meet in the middle.

From the top down, the direction was quite clear for a long time. If we want robotics to scale the way language models did, we can't keep collecting data for every single robot separately and training a separate model for each one. That's too slow and too expensive. So at the leadership level there was a strong belief that we need one model that works across many embodiments, and that data from one robot should benefit another. That's the north star. It tells everyone what problem matters.

But a north star alone doesn't tell you how to get there. The actual mechanism, how you make knowledge transfer between robots with different arms, grippers, kinematics, and camera setups, came very much from the bottom up. Researchers on the team ran many experiments, mixed datasets in different ways, tried different representations and training recipes, and noticed that under certain conditions skills learned on one platform started to show up on another platform that had never been trained on that task. That's not something you can plan in a roadmap. You discover it by getting your hands dirty.

Once that signal appeared, the top-down part came back in. Leadership recognized it and put more resources behind it, more compute, more data collection, more people, and integrated it into the main model effort. That's when an interesting finding becomes a real capability.

So my view is that the top-down direction sets the ambition and makes sure the organization is aligned on the important problems, while bottom-up research supplies the surprises, the things nobody predicted. A healthy lab needs both. If it's all top-down, you lose creativity and you only find what you already expected. If it's all bottom-up, you get many nice papers that never add up to something bigger. The magic happens when leadership is flexible enough to notice a bottom-up breakthrough and then scale it quickly.

r001.rationale: The response says top-down leadership set the cross-embodiment goal, while bottom-up experiments discovered the mechanism for transferring skills between robots.

r002.rationale: It describes experiments by researchers on the team and later support for the finding, but does not say Motion Transfer arose from integrating compatible ideas from multiple research teams into one system.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think Motion Transfer is a good case study in how those two things have to coexist, because neither one alone would have gotten us there.

The top-down part was the conviction that robots should learn skills from human motion, not from hand-designed controllers or reward functions that we spend months tuning for every single behavior. That was a bet. It came from looking at where the field was going, seeing what was happening with large models and data in other domains, and saying, we need a general pipeline where you capture a person moving and a robot can do that. If you don't set that direction, people drift toward incremental wins on the benchmark they already have.

But the bottom-up part is where it actually became real. A lot of the hardest problems were things nobody planned. Retargeting from a human body to a quadruped or a humanoid with totally different kinematics, dealing with noisy motion capture, bridging the sim-to-real gap when the dynamics don't match. Those were solved by researchers who were deep in the details, trying things, failing, noticing something odd in a plot, and following that thread. I couldn't have specified those solutions from above. I didn't know what they were.

So the way I think about it is that top-down sets the question and protects the space for it. It says this problem matters, here's roughly what success looks like, and we're going to keep investing even when the first versions look clumsy. Bottom-up supplies the answers and, often, reshapes the question. We started with one idea of what motion transfer meant, and the research pushed us toward something broader than we intended.

The failure modes go both ways. Too top-down, and you get people building toward a demo instead of toward understanding. Too bottom-up, and you get a dozen clever papers that don't compose into anything. The job of someone leading this is mostly to keep those two in tension, and to be willing to update the direction when the bottom-up signal is telling you something you didn't want to hear.

r001.rationale: It says top-down direction sets the question and what success looks like, while bottom-up research supplies answers and reshapes the question.

r002.rationale: It describes researchers solving practical problems, but does not say that Motion Transfer arose by integrating compatible ideas from multiple research teams into one system.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. Top-down direction gives us a goal: what capability do we want the robot to have, and why does it matter? But it doesn’t necessarily tell us how to get there. That’s where bottom-up research comes in—trying ideas, understanding what works, and letting the results challenge our assumptions.

For Motion Transfer, the broad goal is to turn motion into useful robot behavior. But the research has to work through the gap between a desired movement and what a robot can physically execute. Those details can reshape the direction itself. So I see it as a feedback loop: the goal guides the experiments, and the experiments help us refine the goal.

r001.rationale: It says top-down direction defines the goal and bottom-up research explores how to achieve it through experiments.

r002.rationale: It describes a feedback loop between goals and experiments, but does not say Motion Transfer integrated ideas from multiple research teams into one system.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as complementary. Top-down direction gives you a goal: what capability do we want, and why does it matter? But that doesn’t tell you which technical approach will actually work. For that, you need bottom-up research—trying ideas, understanding failures, and letting the results challenge your assumptions.

For Motion Transfer, the important thing is to keep that feedback loop open. The broader goal guides the experiments, but what you learn from the experiments should also reshape the direction. If everything is dictated from the top, you can miss unexpected opportunities. If everything is bottom-up, you can end up with interesting results that don’t come together into a useful capability.

r001.rationale: It says top-down direction sets the goal and bottom-up research tests approaches, learns from failures, and challenges assumptions.

r002.rationale: It discusses feedback between direction and experiments but does not say Motion Transfer integrated compatible ideas from multiple research teams into one system.
